questions.question: Solve T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n using Master Theorem.
questions.solutionApproach: a=3, b=2, f(n)=n. n^(log_2 3) ≈ n^1.585. f(n)=n grows slower than n^1.585 → Case 1. T(n)=Θ(n^(log_2 3)).

questions.question: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n.
questions.solutionApproach: a=2, b=2, n^(log_2 2)=n^1=n. f(n)=n log n is asymptotically LARGER than n but not polynomially larger (only by a log factor) — this is the boundary case NOT covered by basic Master Theorem. Use recursion tree: at depth k, work = n log(n/2^k), summed over log n levels gives T(n)=Θ(n (log n)²).
questions.answer: T(n) = Θ(n (log n)²) — classic 'extended Master Theorem' boundary case.

questions.question: int f(int a[], int n) { if(n<=1) return a[0]; int m = f(a,n/2), rest_work; for(int i=0;i<n;i++) rest_work=i; return m + rest_work; }  Set up the recurrence for this function's time complexity.
questions.solutionApproach: One recursive call on n/2, plus O(n) loop work. T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n).
questions.answer: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n)  → solves to Θ(n) by Master Theorem Case 3.

questions.question: void h(int n) { if(n<=0) return; h(n-1); h(n-2); h(n-2); }  Set up the recurrence for the number of calls to h().
questions.solutionApproach: One call on n-1, two calls on n-2, plus 1 for the current call. C(n) = C(n-1) + 2C(n-2) + 1.
questions.answer: C(n) = C(n-1) + 2C(n-2) + 1 — exponential growth (faster than plain Fibonacci due to the extra n-2 call).
